title: Every Gate: A RISC-V Core Paints a Mandelbrot
subject: Claude designs a 5-stage pipelined RISC-V CPU (RV32I plus MUL/MULH) entirely out of 2-input logic gates and flip-flops, then simulates every gate on every clock cycle while the core runs a real fixed-point Mandelbrot program. A golden ISA model checks each retired instruction in lockstep, and 6 workers deliberately break gates to measure stuck-at fault coverage.
why_hard: Claude has to write the hardware itself, as a netlist generated by small HDL-style JS functions, and every bit has to be right. If one gate is wrong anywhere, the Mandelbrot visibly corrupts and the lockstep checker flags it. The core needs Kogge–Stone adders, a 5-level barrel shifter, a Baugh–Wooley signed multiplier with a Dadda reduction tree, a 31×32 flip-flop register file with 32:1 mux read trees, an immediate generator, byte-lane load/store logic, forwarding, load-use stall detection, BTFN branch prediction and flush logic, all from AND/OR/XOR/NOT/NAND/NOR/MUX primitives. The netlist must be levelized and compiled into straight-line JS that runs tens of millions of gate evaluations per second. Claude also has to write an RV32 assembler and the Mandelbrot program in assembly, run the ISA golden model in lockstep, and build bit-parallel fault simulation (31 faulty machines per 32-bit word) across Web Workers. On top of that, a WebGL floorplan draws every gate as a cell that lights when it switches. The layers depend on each other: none of it can be faked, and if one layer is broken, everything above it breaks too.
angle: Opus 5.5 at maximum effort, no libraries: hand-written WebGL and canvas 2D, Web Workers, one night
science:
1) NETLIST. Primitives: NOT, AND2, OR2, NAND2, NOR2, XOR2, XNOR2, MUX2 (counted as 1 cell, NAND2-equivalent weights INV 0.67, NAND/NOR 1, AND/OR 1.33, XOR/XNOR 2, MUX2 2.33) and DFF (positive edge; enable and synchronous reset built from a MUX2 in front). Generators in JS (wire(), gate(), bus(n), adderKS(n), mux(n), decoder(k), reg(n,en,rst)) produce arrays type[], inA[], inB[], inS[] plus a module tag per net. Blocks:
- IF: PC register (32 DFF), PC+4 incrementer, next-PC mux {PC+4, ID-predicted target, EX-redirect target}.
- IF/ID register.
- ID: full RV32I+MUL/MULH decoder (opcode/funct3/funct7 to control bits); immediate generator for I/S/B/U/J; register file of 31×32 DFFs (x0 hardwired to 0), a 5→32 write decoder, and two read ports built as 32:1 trees of MUX2, with a WB→ID internal bypass. Hazard unit: stall if ID/EX.memRead && ID/EX.rd≠0 && (rd==rs1 || rd==rs2), which freezes PC and IF/ID and inserts a bubble into ID/EX. Branch prediction is BTFN: for B-type with imm[31]=1, predict taken and redirect from ID with a dedicated target adder (1 bubble). JAL is redirected in ID.
- ID/EX register.
- EX: forwarding muxes A/B (select EX/MEM.rd match first, then MEM/WB.rd match, rd≠0, gated by the FORWARDING control input; when it is off, the hazard unit stalls on any RAW instead). ALU: 32-bit Kogge–Stone add/sub (5 prefix levels), SLT/SLTU from the carry and sign, AND/OR/XOR, and a 5-stage logarithmic barrel shifter (SLL by bit-reversal; SRA via sign fill). Multiplier: 32×32 Baugh–Wooley partial products, a Dadda tree of full and half adders (FA = 2 XOR + 2 AND + 1 OR), and a 64-bit Kogge–Stone final adder; MUL returns bits 31..0 and MULH returns bits 63..32. Branch comparator (EQ/NE/LT/GE/LTU/GEU). On a mispredict or JALR, flush IF/ID and ID/EX and redirect the PC.
- EX/MEM register; MEM: byte enables, store-data lane replication, load alignment and sign/zero extension for LB/LH/LW/LBU/LHU, SB/SH/SW.
- MEM/WB register; WB: result mux {ALU, MUL, load, PC+4}.
Instruction ROM (16 KiB at 0x0000_0000) and data RAM (64 KiB at 0x0001_0000, framebuffer at 0x0001_8000) are behavioral arrays at the netlist ports. The UART TX is a store-byte to 0x2000_0000. Everything else is gates. FENCE, ECALL and EBREAK decode as NOPs; there are no CSRs or traps.

2) SIMULATION. Topologically sort the combinational gates; DFF outputs and memory read data are level 0. Logic depth L(g) = 1 + max(L(inputs)). Compile to one straight-line JS function in Int32Array form (s[g]=s[a]&s[b]; MUX: s[g]=(s[a]&~s[c])|(s[b]&s[c]); NOT: ~s[a]). Each net is a 32-bit word, so 32 machines run in parallel. One cycle: (a) drive the memory read ports from register outputs: imem[PC.Q] and dmem[EXMEM.addr.Q]. Both addresses come straight from flops, so a single evaluation pass is exact. (b) Evaluate all gates in level order. (c) Rising edge: every DFF Q←D, and memory writes commit. Toggles(cycle) = popcount over lane 0 of (s_new XOR s_old), counted per module. Activity α = toggles / (nets × cycles). Estimated dynamic power P = ½ · toggles/cycle · C · V² · f with C = 1.2 fF, V = 0.9 V, f = 500 MHz, labelled "est.". Static critical path = max L over flop D inputs and memory ports, traced back gate by gate (expected through fwdA → Baugh–Wooley → Dadda → KS64 → WB mux). The dynamic depth is the deepest level that toggled this cycle. Measured throughput = gates × cycles/s.

3) GOLDEN MODEL. An RV32I+MUL/MULH interpreter written independently of the netlist runs the same ROM. Each time a valid instruction leaves WB, compare (pc, rd, wdata, store addr/data) against one golden step. The divergence counter must stay 0, and the first divergence would be logged with both states.

4) PROGRAM (assembled in-page by a hand-written two-pass assembler). Mandelbrot in Q4.28 fixed point. Fixed multiply: x·y = (MULH(x,y) << 4) | (MUL(x,y) >>> 28). Iterate z←z²+c while |z|²<4 (the constant 4.0 as 0x4000_0000) up to MAXIT, and store the iteration count as a byte at FB + y·W + x. W×H = 48×32, tuned so one frame takes ~30–40 s at the measured clock. After each row the program prints "r=NN it=NNNNN" through the UART; after each frame it prints a byte checksum, halves the scale from a view table in RAM (centre −0.743643887, 0.131825904) and starts the next frame. The display only maps byte values to colours.

5) PERFORMANCE COUNTERS (read from pipeline nets, not the ISA): cycles, instret, IPC = instret/cycles, CPI, load-use stalls, flushes, branch accuracy = correctly predicted conditional branches / all conditional branches, and forward counts from EX/MEM vs MEM/WB.

6) FAULT SIMULATION (6 workers). Universe: stuck-at-0 and stuck-at-1 on every gate output net (2 × nets). Each batch draws 31 random faults without replacement. Lane 0 is the good machine and lanes 1–31 each carry one fault. A batch-specific compiled function forces faulted nets with s[g]=(s[g]&~m0)|m1, where the masks hold the lane bit. Primary outputs (imem addr, dmem addr, wdata, byte-enables, we, retire-valid) are compared each cycle against lane 0. A lane that differs is DETECTED (its detection cycle is recorded) and dropped. Memory read data from lane 0 is broadcast, which is valid because undetected lanes still have identical bus outputs. The test runs 4096 cycles of the same program. Coverage = detected / simulated, with a Wilson 95% interval as the estimate for the full universe, reported per module. Undetected faults are mapped back onto the floorplan.

ON-SCREEN NUMBERS: gate and DFF counts per module, NAND2-equivalents, logic depth, toggles per cycle and α per module, est. mW, cycle and instret counters, IPC/CPI, stall and flush counts, branch accuracy, forward counts, register values in hex, the instruction in each pipeline stage, bus values on wires, cycles/s and gate evals/s, golden divergences, fault batches, coverage ± CI, mean detection latency, framebuffer progress (pixel, row, frame) and UART output. Every one of these is computed by the code described above.

design.layout: A full EDA editor on the 1920×1080 stage with 8 px margins and gutters. A top status bar sits above a left dock (controls and netlist hierarchy), a big centre canvas (the die floorplan, where every gate is a cell), and a right dock (architectural state: registers, pipeline, program output). A bottom dock spans the width with a logic-analyzer waveform timeline, the fault-simulation campaign and machine resources. It fits the subject because chips are actually designed in this kind of tool, and the waveform viewer works naturally as a bottom timeline. It is also structurally different from the three-column grids of projects 1–3.

design.feel: An IC layout viewer at 2 a.m.: a pure black canvas with saturated mask-layer colours (metal-1 blue, metal-2 magenta, poly red, diffusion green, via gold), a GTKWave-style logic analyzer, and datasheet-dense tables. The whole die shimmers as cells flicker with switching activity, while the right dock calmly shows the architectural truth: registers, the pipeline and a Mandelbrot slowly painting.

mid_work: There are two layers of prewarm, with no boot screen and no empty state. (1) In code: on load the sim worker builds and compiles the netlist and then free-runs the gate-level core with no throttling for the first ~8 s (the golden model stays in lockstep the whole time). The waveform ring buffer (256 cycles), pipeline diagram (24 cycles), disassembly trace, UART console, IPC/toggle histories and per-module stats fill within the first second of simulated time. All 6 fault workers start immediately, so the coverage curve and its CI band already have hundreds of faults behind them. All charts are drawn from real history buffers only. The first paint happens after the buffers are full. (2) The recorder's 30 s warmup: by then the CPU has finished painting Mandelbrot frame 1 (visible as a thumbnail and its UART checksum line) and is part-way through frame 2. The video therefore opens with the core visibly painting rows of a zoomed frame, the die flickering, the logic analyzer scrolling and the kit's resource charts carrying 30 s of history.

post_angle: Overnight, Claude designed a CPU out of nothing but logic gates. It's a 5-stage RISC-V pipeline with forwarding, branch prediction and a hardware multiplier, {gate_count} gates in all, and it runs on my laptop one gate at a time at {sim_hz} Hz until it paints a Mandelbrot. Every square on screen is a single gate that lights up when it switches. A separate reference model checked all {instret} retired instructions and found {lockstep_divergences} disagreements. Meanwhile 6 workers broke gates on purpose to see whether the chip would notice: {fault_coverage} fault coverage. Project 4 of Pushing Claude to the edge, with no libraries, just Opus and a blank canvas.
